Mr. THOMAS VIEN (Lotbiniere) presented the fifth report of the select standing
committee on Banking and Commerce, as follows:
Whereas the subject of rural credit was referred to this committee for further consideration; and
Whereas the Banking and Commerce committee of the year 1924 in its investigation into questions of credit reported that it found a lack of credit facilities for farmers at rates, and upon terms, suited to agriculture and upon conditions such as obtain in competing countries; and
Whereas it is essential to deal with the serious condition of agriculture consequent thereon:
Therefore be it resolved, that the attention of the government be called again to this important matter, with the urgent request that legislation be brought down at this session for the establishment of an adequate rural credit system.

speechtext:
It is my duty to inform
the House of the resignation from the ministiy of the Solicitor General (Mr. McMurray). The following communications will give to the House the reasons which have caused the Solicitor General to tender his resignation and His Excellency to accept it:
Office of the Solicitor General of Canada
Ottawa, May 20th, 1925.
Dear Premier King:
Matters of a professional and private nature induce me, after careful consideration, to tender you my resignation from your government.
In asking you to accept my resignation permit me to express my thanks for being honored with the appointment of Solicitor General and a seat at your Council Board; also accept my deep appreciation for many personal acts of courtesy and kindness.
I avail myself of the opportunity to express my deep regret in disassociating myself from your self and colleagues with whom I had such cordial relationship.
May I urge for reasons above recited that I bo relieved from my duties as a member of the government and as Solicitor General at as early a date as possible.
Sincerely yours,
E. J. McMurray.
My reply was as follows:
Prime Minister's Office Canada
Ottawa, May 21, 1925.
My dear McMurray :
It is with sincere regret that I have received your letter of yesterday stating that, owing to matters of a professional and private nature, you wish to be relieved from your duties as a member of the government and as Solicitor General at as early a date as possible.
Your letter confirms the representations you have already made to me in conversation. Were it not that the reasons which impel you to desire to be relieved of your present public responsibilities are of the character to which you refer, and that we have already talked the matter over very fully, I should be most unwilling to have you sever your connection with the government. I realize, however, from what you have said to me, how considerable in many ways are the sacrifices, both professional and personal you have made in placing vour time and abilities so exclusively at the service of the public. In the circumstances I have felt I had no
Marine Insurance

alternative but to meet your wishes, and have accordingly tendered your resignation to His Excellency.
I have read your letter to the other members of the government and they desire to join with me in expressing our united regret at your withdrawal from the ministry. May I be permitted to add my own vpry grateful appreciation of your loyal and helpful co-operation in the work of the administration ever since you became a member of it, and of the enjoyment of the closer personal relations which this association has afforded.
Yours very sincerely,
W. L. Mackenzie King.
Hon. E. J. McMurray, M.P.,

speechtext:
Is it the pleasure of
the committee to take up the appropriations in this vote item by item?

Item by item.
Beaumaris-repairs to wharf, $1,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. H. KING (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
I think if hon. members will glance
over the list of items that go to make up the total of this vote, they will see that these items are largely for repairs and replacements or improvements. There is an increase this year in the vote over last year. That is largely made up of three or four items, namely, the harbour of Goderich where there is an increase of something like $80,000 over last year; the harbour of Oshawa, where there is a new work that was approved of by parliament in a vote last year; and the work at Port Maitland. Port Maitland was formerly under the control of the Department of Railways and1 Canals, but it has been transferred to the Public Works department. The work

Supply-Public Works
being done there is necessary to maintain the harbour. Finally there is Port Stanley; there is also an increase under this head, but the work to be done there is essential.

What are all these
for? Are they new votes, or are they simply the ordinary " pork-barrel " votes?

I made the statement just a moment ago that I thought members in glancing down the list would find the items to be largely for improvements of harbours, or replacements and repairs. As we go on, that statement will be found to be correct. The first item is a small amount of SI.000 for repairs to a structure on lake Muskoka, which is used largely during the tourist season. The larger ships using the wharf are those owned by the Muskoka Lake Navigation and Hotel Company, the Archer Lines Lake Service Company and the Muskoka Lake Navigation Company. These boats not only serve the local people but provide connection with the National and Canadian Pacific Railways.

Item agreed to.
Blind River-dredging. $47,000.

['I made the statement just a moment ago that I thought members in glancing down the list would find the items to be largely for improvements of harbours, or replacements and repairs. As we go on, that statement will be found to be correct. The first item is a small amount of SI.000 for repairs to a structure on lake Muskoka, which is used largely during the tourist season. The larger ships using the wharf are those owned by the Muskoka Lake Navigation and Hotel Company, the Archer Lines Lake Service Company and the Muskoka Lake Navigation Company. These boats not only serve the local people but provide connection with the National and Canadian Pacific Railways.']
There is an increase here of 125,000.

This amount is
required to complete a contract for dredging entered into in 1924-25. The contract which was awarded to Messrs. A. B. McLean and Sons, is for the dredging of a channel, 9,260 feet in length, and 150 feet wide, to a depth of 16 feet. The contract was made late in the fall, and we are asking this year for a vote of $47,000, of which $22,000 is a revote. The amount is required to complete the contract.
Could the minister tell us when the work was first commenced on this river, and what the total expenditure has been up to date?

Yes. There has
been construction work done there amounting to $48,855.86, repair work amounting to 84843.41, and dredging amounting to $60,019.91.
Sixty thousand dollars
Yes, for dredging.
Where is Blind River
In East Algoma.

I notice that the item says
there is a revote of $22,000.
Yes.

The only amount down for
Blind River is "wharf reconstruction, $10,000."
There was a supplementary vote last year of $25,000.

Could the minister give
the committee some information as to what is sought to be achieved by this expenditure?

Blind River is
principally a lumbering town; large lumbering operations are carred on there. Its population is about 1,500, and its shipments by water consist of 20.000,000 feet board measure of pine lumber per annum, and the import of about 600 tons of general merchandise. Shipments were treble this quantity, and this factor of the waterborne commerce of the place will undoubtedly revive. About 200 tons of fish are landed at the government wharf and shipped to eastern points by the Canadian Pacific Railway.
What causes such a large expenditure for dredging there? I would have thought there was deep water at Blind River, and a pretty good harbour.

The engineer's
report says:
Its object is to provide a safe channel for boats leaving the wharves of McFadden Limited, with cargoes of lumber, with a depth of 16 feet below mean low water or elevation 580 feet above the sea level, which is the standard improvement plane used on other dredging improvements in this district. The foreshore is comparatively shallow owing to the existence of a large deposit of sand known as the Blind River bank, which stretches easterly from the mouth of the Mississauga river to a point near Algoma mills a distance of about 10 miles and extends into the lake for an average distance of about 2 miles. The greater portion of it is from 12 to 15 feet deep, and its outer margin slopes quickly to deep water. The channel opposite Blind River through this bank is about 7,000 feet long by 150 feet wide.
That is a channel we are making through the bank.
How has the channel been protected there?

No protection has been provided.
Mr. BO.YS: Is it not the experience that the channel fills in every year?
Not every year.
What depth of water is there six hundred feet out?

You go out seven thousand feet to the banks, and then you get deep water.
Supply-Public Works
Is it seven thousand feet from the mouth of the lake before you get into deep water?
No. These banks form out in the lake, as explained in the statement I have just read.

A "bank" means something
out of the water. Is this out of the water? Is it sand that drifts out of the river and is deposited? Surely you do not have to go through seven thousand feet in a channel, a hundred and fifty feet wide.

Banks are forming in lakes and rivers, and in the course of time they come to the surface. It is not an unusual thing in these harbours that a drift from the river qr lake forms this deposit. I am informed the bank is about thirteen feet below the surface and the depth is supposed to go to sixteen feet
At the shallowest point you have thirteen feet?
Yes.
Is there anything on file to show whether or not the engineer considered piers were necessary for protection from the drifting of sand?

No, the engineers have not reported on that. The last dredging was done in 1913 and the channel has been maintained more or less since. It is probably considered cheaper to dredge under those conditions.

Is this work considered
necessary on account of the lowering of the water rather than on account of the drifting of the sand?

Yes, that is the
fact.

How is it there is a
re-christening of the vote? It appeared first in 1922, in the first estimate the government brought down in that year, and it was called "wharf reconstruction." In the estimates of 1923, for the year 1924, it retained that name. The wharf was still being reconstructed. At the time of the 1925 estimates the wharf was not reconstructed and $10,000 more was put in to do the work; ibut in the supplementary estimates $13,000 more was added to get that wharf reconstructed. Then in 1926 the minister has taken it into 'his family under a new title, has christened it "dredging" and has raised the vote this year to $47,000. What is the reason? Was it feared by the govern-

ment that if they put in a dredging vote in the first place, other members would want dredging in their constituencies also, and the government wanted to keep the estimates all looking like repairs and reconstruction?

My hon. friend
knows that is not right.

He does not know it
yet.

The item must
show specifically what the work is for. It is for reconstruction of the wharf, and that work continued during 1923 and 1924. If the item were for dredging the Auditor General would not for a moment consider it as reconstruction or wharf construction. They are two distinct votes.

Why is it that this
was called "wharf reconstruction" last year, as appears on page 39 of the Estimates of 1924, an amount of $21,000? In 1923 the same item was voted for wharf reconstruction. This year, as I say, $47,000 is voted for dredging which, it is stated, corresponds with the amount voted last year for the same work.
That was dredging.

No, it is dredging this
year.

And dredging
last year.

Then it should have
been called dredging.

I thought it
was. I am surprised at that.

Look at page 40 of the Estimates of last year. It still had the old name, " Wharf reconstruction," and what was wharf reconstruction last year is not a new work, but it is called "dredging" this year. When did the transition take place, and why was it not put under the proper heading at that time?

I am surprised
that it is so. I have not the estimates of last year before me, but it should have been "dredging," that was the intention.

I will send a copy of
last year's Estimates across to my hon. friend. This was wharf construction last year the same as the year before.

In the supplementary estimates you will find for Blind River the item,

Supply-Public Works
Dredging $25,000; so that it must have been changed when it came in the supplementaries.

In the supplementaries
last year the vote was $25,000, and then we voted last year Reconstruction, $10,000; so that we had a total vote of $35,000 last year.

I think that
explains the situation. The vote in the supplementaries is for dredging that is being continued this year.

How much has been
spent on the wharf?
Construction expenses, $48,000; repairs, $4,000, and dredging, some $00,000, making a total of about $113,000.

In what
year was the work started and what was the nature of the work in the first year?

This goes back
many years. I have a description of a warehouse built in 1905, and in 1908, due to heavy traffic resulting in an increased' number of activities, an extension was made to the warehouse. I imagine the record goes back further than that. I have not the record here; it would be in the department.
When was it found necessary to commence dredging?
The last dredging prior to this was done in 1913. I imagine there has been dredging there from time to time for many years.
Surely the engineers could give the minister some idea just how permanent an undertaking this dredging is to be, and whether it will be necessary to dredge every year?
The last dredging was done in 1913. We now find it necessary to remove certain debris. That is not a bad record for a harbour on the lakes.

How much
was voted in 1913 for dredging?

There was an
authorization by order in council of a contract to a company to remove 57,197 cubic yards in 1912 and 17,480 cubic yards in 1913.
What company?

The C. S. Boone
Dredging and Construction Company, of Toronto.
What was the cost?

I have not the
cost here.

It is rather difficult to come to any conclusion as the minister's information is rather vague. Although he claims that no dredging was necessary from 1913 until last year, $25,000 was voted last year for dredging, and the minister this year asks for a vote of $47,000 additional for dredging. The dredging business seems to be looking up. How long are we going to have to continue this expenditure?

My hon. friend is not quite right. Last year $25,000 was voted. The estimates were late in being passed and a contract was not entered into until late in the fall. Of the amount voted last year $3,000 has been expended. This year we are asking for $47,000, of which $22,000 is a revote, money unexpended last year.

Even at
that, how long are we going to have to vote $50,000-for $3,000 last year and $47,000 this year make $50,000. Is this to be a permanent annual vote, or shall we have to have another election before we have another vote?

It is hoped this
amount will clean up the contract. It is not an annual affair.

Is the dredging to be
done ly contract or by the departmental engine tis?
By contract.
What is the name of the contractor, and the total amount?

The vote should have been asked several years ago for the dredging of this channel. Lumber boats have been coming out of there for the last four years drawing only about eleven or twelve feet of water when they should be loaded to sixteen feet. This has increased the cost of carriage very much. I can warn the government and the House that, owing to the rapid lowering of lake levels, dredging on the Great Lakes within a very few years is going to be something enormous. This is only a sample of what you are going to get. The lake at that point is some three and a half to four feet lower than it was five or six years ago. In order to make a fund for expenditures of this nature, I would be in favour of going back to the old system of charges: canal tolls, harbour dues and dock dues. I do
REVtSED EDITION
Supply-Public Works

not see why the steamboat men have any right to use the lakes as they are doing now any more than the railway companies would expect the government to build a railway and then allow -them to run their trains over it. As regards this port, if you are going to carry on the trade of this country, you will have to do some of this dredging. The old warehouse on the dock was blown down some five or six months ago, and the next item is to cover reconstruction of that warehouse.

The contract was entered into, October 9, 1924, with A. B. McLean and Sons, Sault Ste. Marie. There were two tenders, the lowest being that of Messrs. McLean at 48 cents per cubic yard, place measurement. The other tender was 75 cents.
How does the price accepted compare with work done by the department?

The cost of work varies in different localities on account of the material, but usually departmental work is on a par with that done by a contractor. We do not figure on a profit or interest or depreciation of plant as the contractor -must do.
Was it not possible to use the departmental dredge in this case?

No. We have
not the plant available for it.

Does the government receive any fees for all these numerous works involving an expenditure of millions of dollars? It is unfortunate that any government ever started such a system. The people who use these rivers and have the advantages of the wharves and warehouses, are just as much under obligation to pay for them as the farmers in the west are under obligation to build elevators. Moreover, this House demands that there shall foe sufficient traffic before branch lines are built. I would be in favour of abolishing these votes altogether. The present system takes up a great deal of the time of this House; it involves the government in millions of expenditure; and nobody gets anything.

No changes have
been made in government policy in connection with the water channels. In the matter of warehousing and wharf privileges, at the larger centres fees are charged but in the smaller localities it would not pay to keep a wharfinger to collect fees, so the people use the wharves there free.
rM>. Carruthers.]
I take it that the minister has a complete statement from the engineer as to the amount of money that will be required to complete the dredging in this harbour.
It is proposed to remove 90,000 cubic yards of fine drift sand at an estimated cost of $43,200, and there will be an allowance for inspection and contingencies.
What will be the depth of the dredging?
Sixteen feet.

I have no personal interest in this vote, nor have I any personal knowledge' regarding the conditions. I want to point out however that a great deal of the emigration from this country to-day is due to the fact that the people in the small localities have not the requirements they should have, especially on the lakes and rivers and on our coasts. The fact is that they are not receiving justice in the matter of public works. We talk about emigration from Canada, and we are spending millions of dollars to bring people into the country. Well, I can take hon. gentlemen dowm to the Maritime provinces and show them there a state of affairs that would sufficiently answer the remarks that have been made about all these votes being cut out. On the shores of the Atlantic and of the gulf of St. Lawrence there are deso'ate villages, from which have emigrated people whose fathers, grandfathers and greatgrandfathers had lived there since this country' was first opened up. They have gone away simply because this and previous governments have not done them justice; they have not been able to secure the improvements which they badly needed. There is one place in particular where two years ago, because this government and past governments as well would not do something in the way of protecting the boats of the fishermen, twenty-five families found it necessary to clear out. These people all left in the fall of 1923, removing to Gloucester in order to make a living. And there are various other places in the Maritime provinces where the same thing has taken place. We are spending millions of dollars on our great ocean terminals, and rightly so; no one wall criticize expenditures of that nature. And we are also faced with a deficit of some $50,000,000 or so in connection with our railways. It is clear therefore that we are not stinting on any of these expenditures. This deficit is due in part to

Supply-Public Works
the low grain rates which we give in the west, while the people of the east are also demanding lower freight rates for their lumber. Now, this is all very well; but why should we not extend some consideration to the small hamlet as well? I do not care how small a village may be, the people who have been born and brought up there are better qualified and in every way better adapted to make a living there than anybody we could bring from Europe or elsewhere. And these people have their rights. I should like to see not only the public works of the country but the postal service as well extend in every way possible the facilities for making life a little more comfortable in the rural communities, especially on our harbours, rivers, lakes and sea coasts.

I would receive with very much sympathy the remarks of the hon. member (Mr. Carroll), but the question here is not as to any hamlet in Nova Scotia or anywhere else, or any small settlement at all. When one makes improvements on the Atlantic coast the thing is done, and no draining of water will render the work futile. But according to the hon. member (Mr. Car-ruthers), who represents the riding in question, this is only the initiation of a tremendously vast expenditure at this and other points, due to a lowering of the lakes. If he is right, then I would presume that we might as well entitle this, " A vote to pfovide water facilities for the city of Chicago"; that is about what it is. Really, the thing is becoming appalling. I listened with amazement to the words of the hon. member, and I do not know that he has exaggerated the situation at all; it seems to me, in view of late events, that the path that confronts us is pretty nearly untraversable. We might as well therefore sit . around a table and see whether we intend to start or not. If we have to continue lowering our canals, improving our docks, and dredging our rivers and lakes even, year after year, at an expenditure of untold millions, the show-down might as well come first as last. I was going to ask, before the hon. member rose, how these people got along before we started an expenditure which has now reached $113,000 and which, with this money now voted, will be $160,000 odd. Of course, the water now is lower than it has ever been. This water wThich is going to furnish power for the people to the south of us comes out of lakes that are the common property of both the United States and Canada, lakes from which neither has the right 219J
to divert any water at all. Has the government really considered the wisdom of calling a halt to all this type of expenditure in order that there might be an object lesson to the world at large as to just what this country is suffering?
Is this Satan rebuking sin?

We might as well
tie up the whole trade of the country.

Well, we are tying it

The hon. member woke

I am sure we all

I have been thinking very seriously that it is the duty of the government-and I am not specially criticizing this government, because, as was remarked by the member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), all past governments have expended money on public works [DOT]-it is the duty of this government, or of the government that succeeds it, to cut out many millions of dollars that are now being expended on various kinds of public works. It may be retorted that a good deal of money has been spent at the head of the lakes, and I admit it.

And more will
be required.

Yes; but it was spent
there of course for the benefit of the country generally. It would be a very good object lesson to our people in the practice of economy if every .possible curtailment of expenditure could be effected, even at the risk to a certain extent of injuring some of our public works already constructed. To-day Canada is suffering from a very heavy burden of taxation, and I believe we need a striking object lesson not only in regard to economy in Dominion expenditure but economy in provincial and municipal expenditure. Out through the western country in many cities, including my own, there has been a determined attempt not to incur further expenditure on public works of any kind for some years to come. As a consequence, in my city the tax rate has been cut down by several mills. I believe the tax rate of the country generally could also be cut down substantially if we made up our minds absolutely to refrain from embarking on new public works that are not absolutely needed, and I would include my own city in this respect, because while there is room for a larger development of the harbours at the head of the lakes, and in the years to come this development will have to be undertaken, yet for the present I believe that enough work has been done there for the public services to be carried on very satisfactorily for a considerable time. I believe the general rule laid down by the previous government has been lived uip to by this government in dealing with requests for new post office buildings, and I think this 
rule should be applied to all classes of public works except such as are absolutely necessary. With regard to new post office buildings, I have had requests for a couple in my riding, but I pointed out that post offices were not being built in other sections of the country, and as a result I got very /little complaint from my constituents, although of course they repeated their requests. I sympathize with this government as I did with its predecessors, who took the attitude that unnecessary expenditure of that kind should not be undertaken. I think it will be well worth while for the minister and the government to very seriously consider this proposition in the interest of the country generally. I am not offering my proposal for drastic economy in any spirit of criticism of the government, because I admit it is trying to live up to the rule laid down by the preceding administration, but our taxation has become so heavy and conditions generally are so depressed throughout the country that I believe it is the duty of every member to impress on the government the urgent necessity of drastic economy in public expenditures wherever this is possible without affecting service to the public.

Mr. Chairman,
I think it is only fair to the department and to the government to call to the attention of the House and of the country the fact that since taking office we have refrained from starting any new. public works. It is true we found certain expenditures were contracted for by the late government, and it was neither wise nor possible for us to cancel those contracts. Generally speaking, this department has simply been trying to hold together our public works, keeping them in repair. This is borne out when I advise the 4 p.m. House in 1913-14 the late government appropriated $48,819,000 for public works; in 1914-15, the first year of the war, $47,154,000; in 1915-16, the second year of the war, $34,599,000; in 1916-17, the third year of the war, $30,828,000; and in 1917-18, the last year of the war, $20,914,000; in 192021, their last year of office, $22,680,000; and in 1921-22 their estimate was $20,609,000. done as the Minister of Public Works. I know that very well because my own section has pressed very heavily at times, and sometimes has got what it has pressed for. Better get used

It is quite true, as the
hon. member for East Algoma says, that the lake levels are down practically three and a half feet from the high point of eight years ago, but the assumption that the lowering of lake levels is entirely due to the diversion of water at Chicago is an incorrect assumption. The right hon. leader of the opposition makes a plea that we should call a halt, put the cards on the table and find out if this is going to go on. The fact is, and I want the House to realize this, that we have had almost as low water in the Great Lakes before, and the engineers on both sides of the line do not attribute over nine or ten inches of the lowering of the level of the Great Lakes to the Chicago diversion. The fact remains, however, that dredging that was sufficient two years ago is not sufficient today because there has been a lowering, and

hon. members from the west must realize that if rates on grain from that very important district represented by my hon. friend from Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) are to be satisfactory, we have to give one hundred per cent carriage to the vessels, which we have not got to-day. All the heavy carriers of grain went through the Soo locks last year loaded to only eighty per cent capacity. The lightship at Sarnia was moved a half mile further out last year, and still boats with a draught of twenty feet bumped at that. The minister is faced with a problem. Mr. hon. friend from Fort William and Rainy River, in making allowances for the government, suggested that pressure was always heavy on the Minister of Public Works. As the representative of a riding with a continuous coast line and a lot of small harbours, where rail communication is not a factor, where the harbour is the only way out for the fisherman and the farmer, I want to say to this House that I know many members on this side have gone to the minister and asked him not to spend all the money that was recommended by the engineering staff. I think members of this House have assisted the Minister of Public Works in his desire not to have too great an expenditure this year. I know it was my pleasure to draw a pencil through two or three recommendations myself, and I think that condition is more general than hon. members from the west realize.
Public works in the Dominion of Canada, on the waterways are a good deal more important than some of us realize. First, there is the movement of our tonnage of grain eastward. Second, there is the moving of coal and general merchandise to the head of the lakes. If you remove, as one of my hon. friends has suggested, this water competition, I do not know what railway rates we are going to have, because water competition has governed railway rates to a very great extent.
There is another respect in which the Great Lakes are important, and it is one which I think should not be lost sight of. Our tourist trade in the central part of this country, as has been pointed out by my hon. friend from Muskoka (Mr. Hammdll) on different occasions, is becoming a very important trade, and it might be interesting to some of my friends to know that at one small point in my riding where we had to spend only eight hundred or a thousand dollars last year on dredgfMr. Malcolm. 1

A summer population of 3,000 has sprung up in this district on lake Huron, and a very considerable amount of American money is left at this point. My hon. friend (Mr. Carroll) said that he could take me to hundreds of little villages that have been depleted as the result of the government not making proper provision to look after these people. All I wish to say in reply is that year by year we are asked to spend millions of dollars in Canada to look after certain interests of these people, and if there are hundreds of settlements still going out of business, what would be the total debt of this dominion if we looked after them all I Our debt in that case would be impossible to compute. If there are settlements in Canada that are depleted to-day as the result of this government not giving them proper facilities, I can show you, on the other hand, in western Canada certain districts that have been depleted as the result of this government spoonfeeding industries for the last fifty years, and if that kind of thing is to continue we will have settlements of this kind all over Canada. I believe the time must come when industries and people requiring the dredging of these streams and the building of wharves must learn to pay their own way, stand on their own feet. There is no question but that Oshawa is one of the large manufacturing towns of Canada, and anyone who visits the place will be confirmed in that opinion. I do not know as to whether the natural physical conditions are there which would warrant a new harbour being dug out or not; that is something that would need examination to say. I certainly think that the existence of business is a justification for water facilities as well as for railway facilities. point. I have no doubt that if the expenditure is justified at all it will result in increasing business. My point was rather as to the necessity of adopting a policy, in the case of harbour construction of this magnitude, of charging dues or fees for the use of the harbour facilities after they are created?

Generally speaking in the case of lake ports very little in the way of harbour dues is collected. But such dues are collected in ports like Montreal, St. John, Halifax and Vancouver. In certain of the larger inland ports also certain dues have been collected. If, after this port is established, the amount of business would indicate that harbour dues should be collected and officials appointed, the harbour will be turned over to the Department of Marine and Fisheries which will appoint the necessary officials and collect such dues as may be determined. But take the harbour of Goderich, where there is a very large tonnage in wheat going through, the collections, as I indicated this afternoon, are practically nil, and that is true largely of the lake ports. In the port of Toronto the harbour commission collects dues. At Port Arthur and Fort William, and other ports of that character the collections by the department are very small. Nevertheless the facilities at these ports give accommodation to the grain fleet and promote the movement of grain through the ports each year.

That was my reason for asking the question. This afternoon the minister stated that at some ports, particularly at [Mr Meighen.]
the smaller points, the amount of business was not sufficient to make it worth while to keep a collector there. But in the case of a harbour serving such an important centre as Oshawa, and which it is admitted will cost anywhere in the vicinity of half a million dollars, I would suggest that it would be sound policy to apply the same rules as are carried out in the case of the ocean ports. I agree with what was said this afternoon in that respect ; that it is simply impossible to keep on adding to the harbour facilities in inland waters to the extent that we are doing today without charging a fee for the service. Frankly I cannot see the justice-and I did not mention it in connection with the small items because I saw the force of the minister's remark in those cases-of the country mortgaging its future to supply harbour accommodation on this scale for any town or any community without making it revenue producing in some respects. I cannot see why dues should be charged in ocean ports and not charged in inland ports of such magnitude as this. Therefore I suggest, if we intend to keep on providing such facilities and spending sums running up into the millions of dollars for the purpose, we will be obliged in self defence to make these harbours revenue producing, to the extent at least that they will carry a portion of the load.

The discussion
in connection with harbours has been very interesting and very instructive. However, I doubt whether the application of the system followed in the case of ocean ports to ports in inland waters will bring about any great results. Much of the traffic developed' in the case of Oshawa will be local. At the same time ships crossing the lakes from United States ports will enter the harbour, as will also vessels passing up and down the lakes. Nevertheless, the tonnage entering the harbour will not be in the same category as tonnage passing in or out Atlantic or Pacific ports. And the dues collected in our ocean ports are largely in line with similar dues in other ports of the world. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) this afternoon indicated that a charge should be made for warehouses erected by the government. It was shown, however, that in the case of Goderich the tonnage amounted to 600 tons. At ten cents a ton for warehousing, which would be a fair charge, the revenue would only be S60 a year. But it 13 said "Why do the people interested not provide the accommodation themselves?" If the people were so organized that these facilities

could be provided through the municipality it would be all right; but if you allow your wharf or other structure to be used by individual steamship lines they immediately take hold of it and make it useful for their own purposes.
If we should adopt the argument advanced by some hon. members on the other side of the House, then we would go back to the days of toll-gates on our roads and bridges, when the people who used those facilities had to pay. I do not think it is the desire of parliament to make a retrograde step of that kind. These harbours and the business that goes in and out of them is all a part of the commerce of the nation, and as far as a development of this character is concerned, if the tonnage is such as we hope it will be, I would be very glad to consider if some revenue could not come to the Dominion treasury from the expenditure made at this point. My right hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, in criticizing the expenditure at Kincardine this afternoon, said that we should not reconstruct that harbour. It was a good harbour before confederation, when the people of Ontario expended large sums of money upon it, and that is true of other harbours. As far as this harbour is concerned, I think it would be a great mistake to allow the works there to go into disuse. There is an important Canadian industry there, producing a hundred tons of salt per day, and if the facilities in the harbour are not maintained that industry will go out of business. I do not think it is wise to suggest that this or any other government in Canada should cease development at the present time. Canada needs development and the introduction of new lines of industry. I think my hon. friend's remarks are quite in order, consideration will be given to them, and when this harbour is developed it will be for the government of that day to consider whether tolls should be properly charged.

When the ocean steamships are enabled to come up from Montreal through the waters of lake Ontario, it will follow as a consequence that the government will be called upon to make seaports of all these harbours now being created in our inland waters, and the minister ought to be preparing himself for such a contingency.

I would hardly expect, if there is only thirteen feet of water in the vicinity of these harbours, that we would ever be called upon to make them seaports; and
I would suggest that if the available tonnage in any port warrants the expenditure of $400,000 or $500,000, a fair charge for the use of these facilities should be made. The comparison drawn by the minister between such ports and municipal undertakings such as bridges and roads is hardly a fair comparison, because as a matter of fact the bridges and roads are built and maintained to a very large extent at the expense of the municipalities. The minister suggests that these ports are largely for local use and paid for, not by the community, but by the country as a whole, and therefore the two situations are not comparable. I believe it would be wise for the government to inaugurate, now or in the near future, the policy that when the tonnage reaches a point which would warrant such large expenditure, it should be distinctly understood that a fair fee should be charged for the use of these facilities. It would have two good effects. In the first place it would be partially self-supporting, and in the second place the government would not receive applications from all kinds of places for large expenditures, if those communities knew that the expenditure would be partially paid for by themselves.
